meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The divinity of Jesus is made a convenient cover for absurdity. Nowhere in the Gospels do we find a precept for Creeds, Confessions, Oaths, Doctrines, and whole carloads of other foolish trumpery that we find in Christianity'?
meta.ogDescription: A modern paraphrase, not Adams's wording. It splices and rewrites two of his February 1756 diary entries. Here is what he actually wrote.

answer.label: Not John Adams — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1735–1826 · second President of the United States
answer.sourceLine: Adams never wrote this sentence. It is a reworded splice of two entries in his diary. On 13 February 1756 he wrote, in the margin, “Thus mystery is made a convenient Cover for absurdity.” On 18 February 1756 he asked where the Gospel requires “Creeds, Confessions, Oaths, Subscriptions and whole Cartloads of other trumpery.” The words “divinity,” “Doctrines,” “foolish” and “Christianity” were added later.

source.heading: What Adams actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Diary of John Adams, entries for 13 and 18 February 1756
The Works of John Adams, ed. Charles Francis Adams, vol. 2 (Boston: Charles C. Little and James Brown, 1850), pp. 4–6
Adams Papers Digital Edition, Massachusetts Historical Society (Diary of John Adams, vol. 1)
Not in either entry. Wikiquote lists it as spurious.

source.excerpt:
[13 February 1756] Major Greene this Evening fell into some conversation with me about the Divinity and Satisfaction of Jesus Christ. All the Argument he advanced was, “that a mere creature, or finite Being, could not make Satisfaction to infinite Justice, for any Crimes,” and that “these things are very misterious.” [In the margin:] Thus mystery is made a convenient Cover for absurdity.

[18 February 1756] The following Question may be answered some time or other—viz. Where do we find a praecept in the Gospell, requiring Ecclesiastical Synods, Convocations, Councils, Decrees, Creeds, Confessions, Oaths, Subscriptions and whole Cartloads of other trumpery, that we find Religion incumbered with in these Days?
trail: Wikiquote lists the exact wording under “Spurious quotations” on its John Adams page ↗ and describes these as “apparent fabrications; derived from statements by Adams, but with significant alterations and additions.” It notes the line was attributed to Adams in William Edelen’s Spirit (1988), p. 4.

The real “convenient Cover for absurdity” line is a margin note in Adams’s diary entry for 13 February 1756 ↗. Its subject is “mystery”: a friend’s claim that the doctrines he was defending were “very misterious.”
The “precept” and “trumpery” half comes from a separate entry for 18 February 1756 ↗. Its list has no “Doctrines,” never uses the word “foolish,” and complains of “Religion,” not “Christianity.”
Both genuine lines appear in print in The Works of John Adams, vol. 2 (1850) ↗, edited by his grandson Charles Francis Adams.
source.excerptNote: This is the Massachusetts Historical Society transcription, with Adams’s own spelling. The 1850 Works prints the same lines in modernized spelling (“cart-loads,” “encumbered”). In neither version does Adams call the divinity of Jesus a cover for absurdity. His target is the appeal to “mystery.”

author.bio: John Adams was a Massachusetts lawyer and revolutionary leader. He served as the second President of the United States from 1797 to 1801. He kept a diary from his youth, and its frank early entries on religion and church authority are the real source behind this popular quotation. His grandson Charles Francis Adams printed the diary in The Works of John Adams (1850).

misattribution.heading: How a diary note became a manifesto
misattribution.intro: The popular version takes two real entries from Adams’s diary, five days apart, joins them, and rewrites them. The changes turn a young man’s complaint about “mystery” and church formalities into a direct attack on the divinity of Jesus and on Christianity.

items.why: “Mystery” becomes the scare-quoted “divinity” of Jesus. “Doctrines” and “foolish” are added. “Religion incumbered with in these Days” becomes “in Christianity.” Compare the 13 February ↗ and 18 February 1756 ↗ entries.
Wikiquote gives this book (p. 4) as where the exact wording was attributed to Adams. It adds that the line “seems to paraphrase portions of two diary entries.” See Wikiquote: John Adams ↗.

items.who: Ernest A. Steadman, Pathway to the Stars (2007)
items.why: Wikiquote records a shorter version, “The doctrine of the divinity of Jesus is made a convenient cover for absurdity,” attributed to Adams in this book (p. 66), and calls it “another paraphrase of the entry for 13 February 1756.” See Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: What Adams actually wrote: “Thus mystery is made a convenient Cover for absurdity” (diary, 13 February 1756 ↗). The “divinity” version is not his wording.

context.heading: Why the rewording matters
lead: The real entries are a private diary from February 1756, written long before Adams entered public life. In the first, a friend has been defending the “Divinity and Satisfaction of Jesus Christ” and falls back on calling these things “very misterious.” Adams notes in the margin that mystery is being used to cover absurdity. Five days later, after an evening of talk about the purpose of Christianity, he asks where the Gospel requires synods, creeds, oaths and “whole Cartloads of other trumpery.”

The popular version keeps the bite but changes its target. It makes Adams dismiss the divinity of Jesus and “Christianity” outright, in words he never used. Arguments about the Founders’ religion often turn on single quotations, so the difference matters. People on every side should quote the diary itself.
detailsBody: “The ‘divinity’ of Jesus is made…” — Adams wrote “Thus mystery is made…” (13 February 1756).
“Nowhere in the Gospels do we find a precept for…” — Adams asked a question: “Where do we find a praecept in the Gospell, requiring…” (18 February 1756).
“Creeds, Confessions, Oaths, Doctrines” — Adams listed “Ecclesiastical Synods, Convocations, Councils, Decrees, Creeds, Confessions, Oaths, Subscriptions.” There is no “Doctrines.”
“whole carloads of other foolish trumpery that we find in Christianity” — Adams: “whole Cartloads of other trumpery, that we find Religion incumbered with in these Days.”

sourcesVerified.claim: The 13 February 1756 diary entry records Major Greene's conversation on the 'Divinity and Satisfaction of Jesus Christ' ("these things are very misterious"), with the margin note 'Thus mystery is made a convenient Cover for absurdity.'

The 18 February 1756 diary entry asks: 'Where do we find a praecept in the Gospell, requiring Ecclesiastical Synods, Convocations, Councils, Decrees, Creeds, Confessions, Oaths, Subscriptions and whole Cartloads of other trumpery, that we find Religion incumbered with in these Days?' It contains no 'Doctrines', 'foolish', 'divinity' or 'Christianity' in that list.

The Works of John Adams, vol. 2 (Boston: Charles C. Little and James Brown, 1850), ed. Charles Francis Adams, prints 'Thus mystery is made a convenient cover for absurdity' (13 Feb.) and the 'whole cart-loads of other trumpery' question (18 Feb.) on pp. 4–6. Checked via the item's metadata and djvu full text.

Wikiquote lists the exact popular wording under 'Spurious quotations' ('Apparent fabrications; derived from statements by Adams, but with significant alterations and additions'). It says the line was attributed to Adams in William Edelen's Spirit (1988), p. 4, and paraphrases the 13 and 18 Feb 1756 entries. It also lists the variant 'The doctrine of the divinity of Jesus...' from Ernest A. Steadman's Pathway to the Stars (2007), p. 66.

The blog post calls the quote spurious, says it was attributed to Adams in Spirit (1988) by William Edelen, and describes it as a paraphrase of portions of two diary entries (13 and 18 February 1756).
